hook_text: Heat a beaker of ice on a flame, and the thermometer stops at zero for minutes. The flame is still on. Where is the energy going?
clip_script: A beaker of crushed ice sits over a burner with a thermometer in it. The reading climbs from minus twenty to zero. Then it stops. For minutes it sits at zero, while the flame keeps burning. The energy has not vanished. It is busy breaking the water particles out of their fixed rows, so none is left to make them faster. Only when the last ice has melted does the reading climb again, up to one hundred. Then it stops again, even longer this time, while the water boils, because tearing particles completely apart into a gas takes about seven times more energy. Those flat bits are the signature of a change of state. And up in Johannesburg, where the air is thinner, the second flat bit sits at about ninety-four degrees instead of one hundred.
visual_style: A whiteboard beaker over a flame with a big thermometer, then a heating curve drawing itself with two flat plateaus, then particles in rows breaking loose.
pacing: A slow first climb, a dramatic pause at zero, then a brisk run to the boiling plateau.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw the heating curve yourself.
